conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been nauseous for two days. After just a few sips of a fizzy lime drink—something I’ve had before—I suddenly felt sick and vomited. Since then, I’ve been dry heaving every 15 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any blood in the vomit? Or abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood in the vomit, but when I made myself vomit a few times, I noticed a little blood on my fingers. I don’t have belly pain, but my stomach muscles are sore from all the heaving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And any fever, chills, or changes in bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a low-grade fever, I think. And I’ve had more bowel movements—about five yesterday, some loose, some normal. No blood in the stool, but I felt urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. You have a history of gastroparesis and a GJ tube. When was your last tube feeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two nights ago. I skipped it last night because I was too nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll start you on IV fluids and anti-nausea meds. We also checked some labs. Your blood work shows a metabolic acidosis, likely from not eating—your body is burning fat for energy, which produces ketones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why I feel so weak? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it gets worse, but we’re treating it with fluids and will restart your tube feeds soon. It should resolve quickly now that we’re supporting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. My blood pressure was high in the ER—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your BP was elevated, but it’s likely due to dehydration and stress. It’s already coming down. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no need for new meds right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my potassium was low last time—did you check that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 3.3, which is a bit low, likely from vomiting. We’ve added potassium to your IV fluids to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been doing this self-vomiting thing because it helps the nausea, but I know it’s not good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand it gives temporary relief, but it can irritate your esophagus. Your recent EGD showed esophagitis and a small ulcer, so we want to avoid further trauma. That’s probably where the blood on your fingers came from.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. So I should stop doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll manage your nausea with IV medications instead—metoclopramide, ondansetron, and a little lorazepam if needed. You’re NPO for now, meaning no food or drink by mouth, to let your stomach rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. What about my tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart them soon, once your nausea is under better control. Nutrition team will guide the timing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea has improved, and labs are trending better. Your acidosis is resolving—your bicarbonate is up to 18 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I can start eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet by mouth, but we’re starting enteral nutrition through your GJ tube today. It’s a concentrated formula to give you calories and help correct the starvation state.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And my stool test came back negative for C. diff, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, good catch. Your stool tested negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and parasites. No infection found, which supports this being a gastroparesis flare, not infectious colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not an infection. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Blood cultures were also negative, so no sign of systemic infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve done well overnight. You tolerated the tube feeds, and your nausea is much better. We’re going to try a clear liquid diet by mouth today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips of water, broth, or apple juice. We’ll go slow—if you keep it down, we’ll advance it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my labs? Is the acidosis gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your bicarbonate is now 23, and anion gap is normal. The starvation ketosis has resolved with nutrition and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such good news. What about my potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium dipped to 3.0 this morning, so we gave a supplement. It’s now 4.5 and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’ve kept down clear liquids, your vitals are stable, and labs are normal. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Are my medications the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home on your usual meds: lansoprazole, levothyroxine, citalopram, and your anti-nausea meds—metoclopramide four times a day now, and ondansetron or lorazepam as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take the metoclopramide regularly. Any diet advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue with clear liquids today, then advance slowly to soft foods. Avoid fizzy drinks and dairy for now—they can trigger symptoms. Restart full tube feeds tonight if tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your PCP in a few days. They’ll monitor your progress and review any pending stool tests, though they’re likely negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep using your tube for nutrition, take your meds, and call if nausea returns or you can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.
